content: The guidelines on the use of antiretroviral drugs for treating and preventing HIV infection were developed with contributions from a wide range of experts and organizations. Key contributors include professionals from the WHO Department of HIV, the Global Hepatitis Programme, the Global TB Programme, and other WHO departments, as well as external consultants and representatives from various international organizations. These individuals provided expertise in areas such as HIV treatment, prevention, and care, as well as operational and clinical guideline development. Administrative support for the development of these guidelines was provided by Valerie Amiel-Fourtas, Jasmin Leuterio, Jane Ndanareh, Laurent Poulain, and Hayet Souissi from the WHO Department of HIV. The guidelines were informed by extensive input from WHO regional and country offices, including experts such as Agnes Chetty (Eastern Mediterranean), Martin Donoghoe and Irina Eramova (Europe), Massimo Ghidinelli (Americas), Naoko Ishikawa (Western Pacific), Frank Lule (Africa), Brian Pazvakavamba (Kenya), Razia Pendse (South-East Asia), Giovanni Ravasi (Americas), and Bharat Rewari (India). The Core Group Chairs for the guideline development were Wafaa El Sadr (ICAP, Columbia University, USA) and Yogan Pillay (Strategic Health Programs, South Africa). Additional contributors included Elaine Abrams (ICAP, Columbia University), Tsitsi Apollo (Ministry of Health, Zimbabwe), Janet Bhila (Y+ Young People Living with HIV, Zimbabwe), Serge Eholié (University of Abidjan, Côte d’Ivoire), and Paul Garner (Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine, UK), among others. The guidelines emphasize the importance of early initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART) for better clinical outcomes and highlight the availability of safer and more effective antiretroviral drugs, including integrase inhibitors, which are becoming more affordable in lowand middle-income countries. They also recommend lifelong ART for all individuals living with HIV, including pregnant and breastfeeding women, regardless of CD4 cell count. Innovative approaches to HIV testing, such as home testing, community-based testing, and self-testing, are also encouraged to expand access to diagnosis and care. The guidelines stress the need for differentiated care models, such as reducing the frequency of clinic visits for stable patients and implementing community-based ART distribution, to improve service efficiency and reduce the burden on healthcare systems. The 2016 consolidated guidelines represent a significant step toward achieving universal access to antiretroviral drugs and ending the HIV epidemic as a major public health threat by 2030. They align with the global health sector strategy on HIV for 2016–2021 and the Sustainable Development Goals, aiming to accelerate progress in HIV prevention, treatment, and care. The guidelines were developed using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach, incorporating evidence from modeling, expert consultations, and country case studies. They are intended primarily for national HIV program managers in lowand middle-income countries but are also valuable for clinicians, policymakers, and organizations involved in HIV care and prevention. The recommendations include new guidance on retesting individuals newly diagnosed with HIV before initiating ART, offering PrEP to high-risk populations, and using alternative first-line treatment regimens, such as integrase inhibitors and reduced-dose efavirenz, to improve tolerability and reduce costs. Operational guidance is also provided to support countries in implementing these recommendations and strengthening the HIV treatment cascade. By implementing these recommendations, countries can achieve greater impact in HIV prevention and treatment, contributing to the global goal of ending the HIV epidemic.
